#2642. “I think I helped him win the Ballon d'Or" – Luka Vušković makes cheeky Harry Kane admission

After England's 2-1 win over Croatia last week, Harry Kane revealed that he had been keeping an eye on Luka Vušković in the Premier League and praised the young centre-back.

Vušković, who faced Kane and Bayern Munich while on loan at Hamburger SV last season, was asked about the England captain's comments by Croatian outlet HRT Sport – and came up with a humorous response.

“It means a lot to me. I think I helped him win the Ballon d'Or too, because he scored about 10 goals against me,” he said with a laugh.

“I'm very glad he won that award because he had an incredible season and deserved it. I'm delighted he said that about me.”

In reality, Kane scored three goals against HSV last season – netting twice in Bayern's 5-0 victory in September 2025 before scoring once more in a 2-2 draw in January 2026.

Just don't expect a repeat performance. Especially this week, with six NFL teams on bye.

Fantasy managers will likely be scrambling to fill holes in their starting lineups − and some of those fill-ins might need to come from the waiver wire. Those who made proactive moves a couple weeks ago to add Chiefs running back Emmett Johnson were rewarded with his 35-point outburst in Week 10.

Could lightning strike twice before season's end?

#2639. Short-handed Warriors struggle without Steph Curry, search for answers

A second-straight blowout loss without superstar Stephen Curry in the lineup has caused the Golden State Warriors to look within themselves for answers.

The Warriors fell to 8-6 after losing three consecutive game, 115-94 against the New Orleans Pelicans at Smoothie King Center on Monday, Nov. 16.

Golden State has gotten off to slow starts in consecutive games. They were down 25-5 with 3:30 in the opening period and finished the quarter with a 35-11 deficit against the Pelicans.

Warriors head coach Steve Kerr said the start "deflated" the team. They had a similar lethargic start in their Nov. 13 matchup against the San Antonio Spurs, where they opened the game with a 38-14 deficit after the first quarter.

"Another terrible start," Kerr told reporters after Monday's loss. "We tried to change it up from San Antonio and change the starting lineup, but just didn't seem to have a lot of juice. We're gonna have to change some combinations and find some things that work for us. We got some good looks early and it was one of those nights where shots didn't go. It felt like that really deflated us, and to lose the quarter, like that, 35 to 11, it's so hard in this league to climb out of a hole like that."

Against the Spurs, they started with Will Richard, Brandin Podziemski, De'Anthony Melton, Yaxel Lendeborg and Draymond Green on the floor. At New Orleans,LJ Cryer and Al Horford were plugged into the starting lineup, alongside Green, Lendeborg and Podziemski.

The piece they're missing is a two-time MVP and four-time champion, often referred to as the greatest shooter of all-time.

Golden State has been without Curry since he exited their Nov. 11 game against the Houston Rockets with 6:25 remaining in the first quarter with an injury that an MRI later confirmed was an oblique abdominal tear. He's expected to re-evaluated in another week, but the Warriors will need to find answers within themselves before then.

This season, the Warriors are 1-3 in four games without Curry who, through 10 games, averages 27.8 points, 3.9 assists and 3.7 rebounds, shooting 50% from the floor and 45.7% on 3-point attempts. Kerr is searching for different lineups up to figure out ways to make up for Curry's absence.

"Without Steph, we've got to mix and match a little bit, and, you know, we'll have to experiment," Kerr said. "Without Steph, obviously, we're looking for different combinations that are gonna click, and we've got to find some combos that provide the shooting and the spacing that we need, and the cutting. It's early in the season, so we've got to experiment as well."

The question that Golden State is looking to answer is the same one they've been asking for years: what do they do in non-Curry minutes? Whether he's not on the floor for rest, or in this case, now due to injury. The Warriors have long looked to answer that question. Early in the season, they'll have to find a solution.

Curry isn't coming back anytime soon and the Warriors need to search deep within for answers.

It will take more than a new haircut from Lendeborg to turn things around. After their loss to the Spurs' where he scored three points on 1-of-13 shooting, Lendeborg decided that a change was needed, it resulted in a new look as he chopped his hair.

Kerr hardly recognized him. Podziemski, who knows all about the power of a haircut, embraced it. Against the Pelicans, Lendeborg bounced back with a 28-point performance on 9-of-23 shooting and a poster dunk on Derik Queen.

Still, it's not enough. The Warriors need more than just their rookie to step up. Green had just two points on 1-of-3 shooting. Horford didn't score taking just four attempts. Cryer had seven points on 2-of-10 from the field. Green took accountability for how the team came out.

"That's on me," he said. "Because I'm the leader and I can't let us come out like that, so that's on me."

Green also said that they can't put pressure on their rookie to lead them. He had a moment of mentorship with Lendeborg late in the game on the bench.

"Depend on him, but lower the expectation," Green said. "It's unfair to make him to step into Steph's role 13 games into his career. Right now we're putting too much pressure on him and it's tough to deal with."

They love his demeanor and approach to game. He's a competitor, Kerr said, but ultimately shared the same viewpoint with Green.

"He's a rookie. This is his first year, and we're putting an enormous responsibility on his shoulders," Kerr said. "He has to go through this.  There's no way around it. You can't cheat your way through that. You have to feel the highs and the lows. You heard his comments the other night. He cares about all this stuff, which is a great sign, but you have to learn how to manage that and how to learn from each situation."

With Curry out – along with a number of others such as Jimmy Butler III, Brandon Williams and Moses Moody – the Warriors don't have lots of room for error.

And without Curry, all eyes are on the supporting cast.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Short-handed Warriors struggle without Steph Curry, search for answers

#2638. Cam Newton has a ‘bold’ prediction on who will win the NFL MVP award this year

There are a number of players who continue to be brought up in the NFL MVP conversation this year but the majority of them are quarterbacks.

The likes of Joe Burrow, Josh Allen, Brock Purdy and Jordan Love are among those to have been discussed as possible winners and they all, in their own right, deserve to be in the running.

However, Cam Newton has now suggested that this year's award may not actually be won by a quarterback.

Speaking on 4th&1 With Cam Newton, he said that his 'bold statement' is that the 2026 MVP 'is not going to be a quarterback'.

Newton explained: "This is my bold statement. I think that this year's MVP is not going to be a quarterback.

"Even though it's easy, I think every week it goes from Josh Allen to Bryce Young, who was mentioned earlier in the year, then you have Jordan Love. He was hearing some MVP noise, but now, tonight, after seeing Joe Burrow, you know, it's… Bro.

"I just think that what we're seeing at this receiver position is something that is setting precedents for what the game of football is going to become more than anything in the near future. And it's in a good place."

It certainly is a 'bold' claim from Newton, especially when looking back at previous NFL MVPs.

The likes of Matthew Stafford, Josh Allen, Lamar Jackson, Patrick Mahomes and Aaron Rodgers have won the award in recent years, with the last non-quarterback winner coming all the way back in 2012.

Running back Adrian Peterson picked up the prize on that occasion when he was playing for the Minnesota Vikings.

The 41-year-old all-time goalscoring king has been held to one goal and three assists in eight games, but he is plus-3. The Caps enter on a two-game win streak, both at home. They rallied for a 4-2 victory Saturday vs. New Jersey.

Ovechkin skated in his 347th comeback win to tie Joe Thornton for second-most in NHL history; the only player with more is Patrick Marleau (352). It was also Ovechkin's 467th win on home ice, which passed Brendan Shanahan for the 11th-most in NHL history. He remains one assist shy of tying Nicklas Backstrom (762) for the all-time franchise lead.

Ovi already obviously leads in goals and points, so he is on the verge of becoming only the fourth player born outside North America to lead his franchise in career goals, assists and points, behind Florida's Aleksander Barkov, New Jersey's Patrik Elias and Ottawa's Daniel Alfredsson.

For tonight, Ovechkin is +200 for a goal and +185 for a helper. In 30 career games against the Kings, he has 13 goals and 13 assists. This will mark his final home game against them. It should be Logan Thompson in net and he's 4-2-0 with a 2.69 GAA and .910 SV. Washington swept the 2025-26 season series.

#2635. Draymond Green defends Yaxel Lendeborg from 'unfair' expectations with Stephen Curry out: 'Too much pressure on him'

Golden State Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg has been sensational to kick off his NBA career. The 24-year-old forward has scored at least 20 points in eight of his first 14 games, and played a significant role in the team's eight-game winning streak early in the year.

But after a three-game losing streak, the Warriors' excellence seems far in the rear-view mirror, especially with star Stephen Curry out multiple weeks with an abdominal tear.

That injury has put even more pressure on Lendeborg to keep producing. While the rookie dropped 28 points in a 115-94 loss to the New Orleans Pelicans on Monday, it was an inefficient night.

At one point in the contest, Lendeborg was spotted on the bench holding a towel on his head. Draymond Green eventually came over to engage in an extended chat with the rookie.

After the contest, Green was guarded about the specifics of that conversation, but did offer some insight on how the team can support Lendeborg with Curry sidelined.

"Depend on him, but lower the expectation," Green said. "It's unfair to him to try to make him step into Steph's role 13 games into his career. Depend on him like we need to, but lower what we are expecting of him to allow him to then just flow into it. Right now, we are putting too much pressure on him and it's tough to deal with in Game 13-14 of your career."

The Warriors played two games since Curry's injury, both losses. In the first, Lendeborg went just 1-for-13 from the field, finishing with three points. On Monday, he dropped 28, but was 9-for-23 from the field, including going 2-for-9 from 3-point range.

Following his 1-for-13 performance against the San Antonio Spurs, Lendeborg admitted he was "f***ed up mentally." That, combined with the rookie holding a towel over his head Monday, shows Lendeborg is taking every loss extremely hard.

Green knows that's not a sustainable response. In order to get the best out of Lendeborg, the Warriors need him to flush the bad games and not allow himself to spiral.

Green knows as much, and is clearly trying to do what he can to mentor Lendeborg as he continues to adjust to the NBA.

#2634. FHSAA Open Division football games: What to watch in second week

Lakeland is making a trip to South Florida for the second consecutive week, this time with an opportunity to clinch a spot in the Open Division semifinals.

The Dreadnaughts shocked No. 1 seed St. Thomas Aquinas in overtime in the first week of pool play. Lakeland can secure first place in Pool A if it beats Chaminade-Madonna and Aquinas beats Venice on Friday, Nov. 20.

Lakeland at Chaminade-Madonna is the headliner of the second week of pool play.

St. Thomas Aquinas travels to Venice, Columbus makes its longest trip of the season when it goes to Raines and West Boca hosts Miami Central.

Here's a closer look at the four Open Division games.

Big Question: Who's going to take control in Pool A?

This is the only Open Division game with two teams that won in the first week of pool play, so the winner will be in pole position to move onto the state semifinals. Lakeland is coming off arguably the biggest win in Florida this season, topping previously undefeated St. Thomas Aquinas 27-24 in overtime. Chaminade had an easier time, beating Venice 35-0 in a game that had a running clock before the midway point of the third quarter. So, who will take control of Pool A? Will it be Chaminade, which gets to play its second consecutive home game? Quarterback Brady Quinn was outstanding against Venice, completing 18 of 21 passes for 395 yards and three touchdowns with no interceptions. Lakeland has won nine in a row and should be riding an emotional high after beating the Open Division favorite on the road. Dreadnaughts quarterback Kelin Hendrix rushed for 128 yards and two touchdowns and threw for 54 yards and the game-winning score.

Recruiting matchup to watch: Chaminade 2028 Tromon Isaac Jr. vs. Lakeland 2027 CB Jordan Young (Pitt commit)

Biggest question: Can St. Thomas Aquinas stop Venice's run game?

This is a must-win game for both teams, as the loser will need a lot of help to have a chance to get into the semifinals. Both teams have to be able to put a difficult Open Division opener in the rearview window. St. Thomas Aquinas had not lost a game since the 2025 season opener and had dominated Lakeland the past two seasons. Venice was shut out for the first time since 2019. On the field, it will come down to which defense does a better job stopping the run. Lakeland had a lot of success, gaining more than 300 yards against Aquinas' defense. Venice's strength is putting the ball in the hands of senior running back Dorien Irving Jones. The FIU commit had 151 of the Indians' 270 total yards of offense against Chaminade. If Venice can have success on the ground — and capitalize in the red zone (something it really struggled with against Chaminade) — this could be a really good game.

Recruiting matchup to watch: Venice 2027 RB Dorien Irving-Jones (FIU commit) vs. St. Thomas Aquinas 2027 LB Levi Champion (Liberty commit)

Big question: How will Raines respond to a loss?

This really is uncharted territory for Raines' players. The last time the Vikings lost a game and then had to play the next week was September 2023. Since then? Zero regular season losses, playoff losses in 2023 and '24, followed by a state championship in 2025. This team has to regroup after a 21-point loss and now has nationally ranked Columbus coming to Jacksonville. A win puts the Vikings right back into the race to be in Open Division semifinals. A loss will make it almost impossible. In fact, if Columbus and West Boca both win on Friday, both teams will lock up a spot in the semifinals. Raines came out well against West Boca and scored on its opening drive but couldn't get things going consistently after that. It won't be easy getting the offense going against the Explorers. Columbus has allowed a total of 40 points in the eight games since giving up 31 points in a loss at Aquinas on Sept. 4. It will be interesting to see how Columbus responds to a five-hour road trip to Raines as it will be first time the team has left South Florida.

Recruiting matchup to watch: Raines 2029 QB Sa'Mon Ellison-Morgan vs. Columbus 2027 ATH A'mir Sears (Miami commit)

Big question: Can Miami Central get its offense going?

Central comes into the second week of pool play having lost three of its past four games. In its four losses this season, Central has scored a total of two touchdowns. Now, it plays a West Boca defense that has allowed just 53 total points. The Bulls allowed Raines to score on its opening drive last week but shut out the Vikings for the final three quarters. Miami Central is playing without starting quarterback James Perrone (Pitt commit). The Rockets made senior running back Nino Joseph the focal point of the offense with both carries and screen passes against Columbus. West Boca's defense had 11 tackles for loss and five sacks against Raines. Senior Jamir Johnson led the way with 10 tackles, three tackles for loss and a sack, while senior Damari Jerry had nine tackles, two tackles for loss, a sack and a pass defended.

Recruiting matchup to watch: Miami Central 2027 RB Nino Joseph vs. West Boca 2027 DB/LB Damari Jerry (Liberty commit)

Clinching scenarios: Chaminade-Madonna will finish first in Pool A if it beats Lakeland and Venice beats St. Thomas Aquinas; Lakeland will finish first in Pool A if it beats Chaminade-Madonna and St. Thomas Aquinas beats Venice.

Clinching scenarios: Columbus and West Boca will both advance to the Open Division semifinals if they both win.

#2632. Spurs' 12-game winning streak: What to know about Victor Wembanyama and the NBA's hottest team

The NBA's hottest team resides in South Texas. After knocking off the Utah Jazz in Salt Lake City on Sunday night, the San Antonio Spurs enter a new week riding a 12-game winning streak — the franchise's longest in more than a decade. Last season featured only two streaks longer than the Spurs' dominant dozen: a 16-game early-season jaunt by the Oklahoma City Thunder (which, as you might remember, these Spurs snapped in the NBA Cup semifinals) and a 13-game run by the Detroit Pistons … who, as luck would have it, will visit the Spurs in San Antonio on Tuesday night.

When a team goes on a winning streak this long, there's plenty of credit to go around. Let's highlight 12 things worth knowing about the Spurs' stampede to the top of the Western Conference — one for each win in the streak! — starting with … I mean, come on, where else can you start?

After the New York Knicks ended his phenomenal third season just short of a championship, Wembanyama entered the summer with a bitter taste in his mouth … and he seems to have entered the new campaign intent on washing it out by devouring everything in his path.

Wembanyama enters Tuesday's action third in the NBA in scoring (a career-high 28.6 points per game) and fifth in rebounding (11.6 caroms a night) while, for the fourth straight season, leading the league in blocked shots (4.3 swats per contest). He hasn't forsaken the 3-point arc, but he's taking a higher share of his shots than ever directly at the rim, and he's converting them at a predictably elite rate, shooting 79.5% in the restricted area — tops among players to take at least 50 point-blank shots.

(Third on that list, by the way? Friggin' Dylan Harper. Don't worry: We'll get back to him.)

Big Vic is averaging — averaging! — 4.64 dunks per game. That's nearly two more flushes per game than last season (2.78), which was already a career high. As tactics go, "Let's get the biggest guy as close to the basket as possible and let him just put the ball into it" seems like a pretty smart strategy, and the Spurs have been reaping the benefits of it, scoring a scorching 126.6 points per 100 non-garbage-time possessions in Wemby's minutes, according to Cleaning the Glass — a mark that would rank head-and-shoulders above the Los Angeles Lakers' league-leading rate of offensive efficiency thus far.

When it comes to "season-opening heaters," most of the attention has gone to the man most responsible for that No. 1-ranked Lakers offense, Luka Dončić — and understandably so. It's worth noting, though, that the big fella is currently on pace to shatter the all-time record for player efficiency rating while leading the NBA in win shares, value over replacement player and total plus-minus; the Spurs have outscored opponents by 257 points in Wemby's 417 minutes, equivalent to a staggering 29.5 points-per-100.

Watch Wembanyama on a nightly basis — not just the "did he just finger-roll from past the free-throw line?!?" highlights, but the possession after possession where he completely warps the opposition's defense and defangs its offense just by standing there — and you come away feeling like the 22-year-old's control of the game is, or at least can be, total.

"Opponents can't really put me in a situation where I can't answer," Wembanyama recently told reporters. "So now all I have to do is not beat myself."

For more than three weeks, he hasn't — and, in a related story, nobody's beaten the Spurs, either.

All right, take it easy there, Thanos. (Not sure if you've heard, but it's all about Dr. Doom right now.)

Generally speaking, if you're in the top 10 on both ends of the floor, you can consider yourself a contender; if you're in the top five on both ends, you're in the inner circle. San Antonio enters Tuesday's action ranked second in the NBA in points scored and allowed per possession, according to Cleaning the Glass.

Where'd the Spurs finish last year, you might ask? Oh, I'm so glad you did. They were … third in points scored per possession, and third in points allowed per possession. If that was good enough to get them to the Finals, maybe bumping up to second both ways will be enough to get them to the top of the mountain this time?

San Antonio has a point differential of +180 for the season — the 21st-highest total ever through the first 14 games of a campaign, according to Stathead. Of the 20 teams above these Spurs, 17 made at least the conference finals; eight of them won it all.

Here's another: The Spurs are blitzing their opponents by 15.2 points per 100 non-garbage-time possessions thus far — the best net rating in the sport. Since the 2003-04 season, only four teams have finished a season outscoring the opposition by more than 12 points-per-100. All four of them — the 2007-08 Boston Celtics, 2014-15 and 2016-17 Golden State Warriors, and the 2024-25 Thunder — went on to win the NBA championship.

According to Jared Dubin's adjusted efficiency metrics at Last Night in Basketball, which measure how much better or worse a team's offense and defense were than the league's average unit in that season, the 2026-27 Spurs currently have a net rating 11.4 points-per-100 better than league average. That ranks third in Dubin's database, which goes all the way back to the ABA-NBA merger in 1976 — behind only Michael Jordan's 1995-96 Chicago Bulls (who won the title) … and this year's Boston Celtics, who (Monday's loss to the Orlando Magic notwithstanding) have been pretty awesome this year.

San Antonio's average margin of victory thus far is 12.86 points per game. Only one team has ever finished a full season higher: the '24-25 Thunder (+12.87) … who, again, won the title.

According to Basketball-Reference's Simple Rating System — a metric "that takes into account average point differential and strength of schedule" — this year's Spurs are 12.75 points better than league average. That's on pace to be the highest SRS rating in Basketball-Reference's database, ahead of teams like the '24-25 Thunder, 1970-71 Milwaukee Bucks, '95-96 Bulls and 1971-72 Los Angeles Lakers — all of whom (say it with me) won the title.

It's early, obviously, and 14 games is too small a sample to draw any definitive conclusions. This much, though, seems clear. If folks start digging into the historical record in search of points of comparison to what you're doing, and they keep coming up with teams that won the NBA championship? You're probably doing something right.

The backcourt logjam that some pundits anticipated last season never really materialized in San Antonio. De'Aaron Fox and Stephon Castle started; rookie Harper mostly came off the bench; the trio shared the floor for just 25 minutes during the regular season and 44 minutes in the playoffs, and the Spurs made it all the way to the NBA Finals. Not actually a problem, right?

Well, that seemed less likely to be the case this season, after Harper authored a breakout performance in his first postseason — and followed it up by making it pretty clear that he wasn't particularly interested in continuing to come off the bench. That led Spurs head coach Mitch Johnson to decide to open this season with all three of his high-octane guards in the starting five, backstopped by Wembanyama with Devin Vassell operating as an ostensible small-ball power forward. The early returns have been explosive:

The Spurs have hammered opponents by 110 points in 141 minutes with Fox, Castle and Harper sharing the floor this season, according to PBP Stats. They're scoring and defending at league-best rates in those minutes … and yes, a lot of that stems from the fact that Wembanyama has been out there for every single one of them. It's also working, though, because the guards are each finding ways to get in where they fit in.

They're flying up the court, with more than 23% of San Antonio's offensive possessions coming in transition in the three-guard lineup, and those units scoring at near-league-best levels on the break. Castle and Harper are almost exclusively taking shots at the rim or from beyond the arc in those minutes, getting to either catch-and-shoot or attack downhill after an initial action bends the defense.

Fox and Castle, both questionable 3-point shooters, have both been knocking down well over 40% of their triples in these alignments. When the pick-your-poison wheel spins to a center guarding Castle, the Spurs have shown their work in developing counters to that scheme.

And while conventional wisdom would warn you against the defensive drawbacks of playing small, with no player listed taller than 6-foot-6 at the 1 through 4 spots, those lineups have rebounded fine, haven't given up a ton of opportunities at the rim, and have yet to be significantly exploited for their lack of size on the perimeter. (It seems that having that French dude back there goes a long way toward bucking conventional wisdom.)

"I understand the narrative around it. I always land on the same reasoning at the very end of it," Johnson told reporters about starting the three guards during the preseason. "They're three of our better players. [...] I think they can dribble, pass, shoot, defend, make winning plays."

Whether they'll continue to do so in this alignment remains to be seen; when offseason signing/veteran power forward Tobias Harris heals up from the calf injury that has cost him the opening month of the season, Johnson will likely have a difficult decision to make. Then again, if the not-so-small-ball Spurs keep blowing everybody's doors off in this look … maybe he won't.

"The biggest thing is, I've got handlers all around me — guys that we want to put the ball in their hands and pick-and-roll around me," Wembanyama said. "That makes things easier."

Since opening the season with losses to the Thunder and Rockets, the Spurs have gotten the opportunity to get right with a pretty friendly stretch of road.

They've had three games against the Jazz, two games against the Kings, and matchups with the Suns and Bulls. They've also caught the Timberwolves without Anthony Edwards or Rudy Gobert, the Mavericks without Cooper Flagg or Kyrie Irving, the Trail Blazers without Ja Morant, and the Warriors right after Stephen Curry went down.

Add it all up, and the Spurs' season-opening slate ranks among the softest in the NBA, according to multiple strength-of-schedule metrics. San Antonio doesn't have to apologize for that, of course. You play the teams that are in front of you, with whoever's in uniform for them when you show up. We've seen plenty of teams fail to capitalize on the opportunity to take down a team at less than full strength. (Looking at you, Mavs.)

Besides, when presented with matchups against shorthanded or sorry opposition, the Spurs have done what good teams are supposed to do: namely, win all of those games, with most of those victories coming by double digits. It's just something to keep an eye on, particularly with a tough opponent like Detroit up next … before three more against the Clippers, Pelicans and Kings. (The games to really keep an eye on? Nov. 27 against Luka and the Lakers, and Nov. 29 against that damn good Celtics team.)

Fox got raked over the coals this summer for his underperformance in the NBA Finals. (Which, it's worth remembering, came with him nursing a high ankle sprain that likely would've sidelined him for weeks had it been the regular season.) His struggles under the brightest lights, combined with Harper's stellar showing in his maiden postseason voyage, primed the pump for the shift to the three-guard lineup, and led to no shortage of calls for the veteran triggerman to cede the stage — and his spot in the Spurs' pecking order — to the rising sophomore.

Well, Fox is still here … and he's kind of threading the needle.

Fox has taken a clear step back in the Spurs' offensive hierarchy, averaging fewer minutes and points per game than he has since his rookie season, and posting far and away the lowest usage rate, time of possession and average number of touches of his 10-year career. He's taking seven fewer field goal attempts per 100 possessions than he did last year.

When Fox shares the floor with Harper and Castle, he's finishing just 15.7% of San Antonio's offensive possessions with a shot attempt, foul drawn or turnover — the kind of usage rate more commonly associated with a complementary player like Isaiah Hartenstein, Toumani Camara or Christian Braun than with a two-time All-Star who has averaged 21 points per game in his career. He's performing well in that reduced role, though.

Fox more frequently takes high-percentage shots — 32% of his attempts are coming at the rim, his highest rate in six years, while corner 3s account for 12% of his shots, a career high — and has almost totally excised long 2-pointers from his repertoire. That, in turn, has led to more efficient scoring. He enters Tuesday's action toting a .551 effective field goal percentage (which accounts for 3-pointers being worth more than 2-pointers) and a .621 true shooting percentage (which factors in 2-point, 3-point and free-throw accuracy) — both of which are by far the highest marks of his career.

He has paired that leaner shot diet with a voracious appetite for freebies, too, drawing shooting fouls on more than 19% of his field-goal attempts — again, a career high. In fact, among 153 players who have logged at least 300 minutes this season, Fox's .496 free-throw attempt rate is the 11th-highest in the NBA, just ahead of free-throw-magnet big men Joel Embiid and Giannis Antetokounmpo.

Pair that just-the-facts-ma'am scoring game with his ongoing facilitation — a team-high 5.8 assists per game, including 33 to Wemby, making them the third-most-frequent assist combo in the NBA thus far — and Fox has managed to continue providing value while still making room for the evolution of the young talent around him. Not bad.

For fans of a certain age, thinking of the Spurs might evoke images of patient, methodical offensive possessions — all entry passes to Tim Duncan on the low block or swing-swing symphonies of "good-to-great" ball movement, where the pace of their play is secondary to the precision of their movements. These aren't your daddy's Spurs, though; these dudes have a predilection toward moving fast and breaking things. Like, for example, you.

In terms of overall pace of play, the Spurs rank just 24th in the NBA, with their average game featuring about 98.8 possessions, according to NBA Advanced Stats. That's due in large part to their defense, though; San Antonio has the longest average defensive possession in the NBA this season, according to PBP Stats. That stands to reason: When you've got to try to figure out how to crowbar open a crevice to attack with Wembanyama menacing along the back line while the likes of Castle and Harper pressure the ball up top, it might take you a little while.

Once the Spurs get the ball, though, they hit the gas. San Antonio has the fifth-fastest average offensive possession this season, and is tied for the fifth-quickest average time to shot, according to Inpredictable.

As noted by the great John Schuhmann, the Spurs lead the NBA in both transition points scored and allowed per game, outscoring opponents by 13 points a night on the break — a massive gap. With their ability to force turnovers, finish possessions with rebounds and advance the ball to all those jet-fueled guards, more than 19% of their offensive possessions come in transition, according to Cleaning the Glass; that's the most in the league. But thanks to their ability to protect the defensive glass, take care of the ball and sprint back, fewer than 12% of their defensive possessions come in transition … which is also No. 1 in the league.

Since at least the start of the 2003-04 season, no team has ever finished the year No. 1 in the league at both generating and preventing transition opportunities. Just another way these Spurs are on pace (ha!) to dispense with conventional wisdom.

Winning the possession battle isn't exactly a revolutionary concept; coaches have been preaching since time immemorial the importance of taking care of the ball on offense and finishing possessions on defense. It's become an increasingly large point of emphasis in recent years, though, as front offices and coaching staffs engaged in the perpetual pursuit of optimization, hunting for every advantage on both ends of the floor. As it turns out, "making sure we get more chances to shoot and score than the other guys" is a pretty solid way to approach things!

The Spurs were pretty good at that last season. When you factor in how many offensive rebounds they pulled in against how many they gave up, how many free-throw attempts they racked up versus how many they conceded, and how many times they turned the ball over compared with how many times they forced opponents to cough it up, San Antonio generated 2.2 more offensive possessions than its opponents per game during the regular season — a good number, but not quite in the upper echelons of the league, like the team that knocked them off in the Finals.

This season, though, the Spurs have tightened the screws virtually across the board. They're grabbing an even higher share of their own missed shots, turning the ball over at the NBA's lowest rate and getting to the free-throw line more frequently, while also forcing more turnovers and curbing their foul rate. Add it up, and through 14 games, San Antonio is generating 7.2 more possessions per game than its opponents — a massive leap over last season, and the No. 1 mark in the league thus far.

Make sure you take more shots on goal than the other guys and you've got a great shot at winning a lot more often than you lose — especially when you put the ball in the hands of dudes who can make those shots. Dudes like …

… the 20-year-old sophomore, whose combination of throwback cool and downhill explosiveness just keeps leaping off the screen pretty much every time you see him.

Harper has responded to his elevation into the starting lineup by continuing to ball out. His usage, free-throw attempt rate and scoring efficiency are all up; his turnover rate is down. Some of that, obviously, comes from more frequently sharing the floor with multiple other high-level ball-handlers, but still: pretty nice to have the guy who's second on your team in touches only coughing it up 8% of the time, one of the lowest rates of any guard in the league.

Coming off that sensational rookie season, Harper is pretty firmly establishing himself as one of the best players in the league when it comes to getting into the paint and finishing on the interior, shooting a frankly bananas 78.6% in the restricted area — better than high-efficiency bigs like Domantas Sabonis, Jarrett Allen, Walker Kessler and Giannis Antetokounmpo. Decent company for a 6-foot-5 sophomore.

Through 14 games, Harper is averaging 18.3 points, 5.5 rebounds, 4.7 assists and 1.0 steals in 31.5 minutes per game, shooting 55% inside the arc, 34% from long distance and 87% from the charity stripe. The list of players to average 18-4-4 for a full season by their age-20 season is just six names long: Magic Johnson, LeBron James, Tyreke Evans, Dončić, LaMelo Ball and Cooper Flagg. Of that group, only Magic shot at least 50% from the field, as Harper is right now.

There's a 7-foot-4 caveat to that, of course. With the exception of rookie Magic playing alongside MVP Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, those other preternatural playmakers didn't have a gravitational force like Wemby pulling attention away from them and opening up opportunities to slash, score and create. But opportunities only matter insofar as you can capitalize on them, and Harper continues to make the most out of his privileged position, perpetually pressuring the defense and looking for all the world like an All-Star in the making — sooner rather than later.

It's not all beer and Skittles in San Antonio, though. As lights-out as the new-look starting lineup has been, moving Harper into the first five has led to some predictable ripple effects in the second unit. The Spurs' reserve corps has a negative net rating for the season, and has — as you might expect — been significantly worse in the minutes when Luke Kornet checks in for Wembanyama, struggling to score even with at least one of Fox, Castle or Harper on the floor.

Some of those struggles might be mitigated by the introduction of Harris, whom the Spurs signed to a two-year, $31 million contract in free agency, and who's yet to play after suffering a left calf strain during training camp. But Johnson will have to shuffle his rotation to make space for the veteran forward. What impact might that have on the minutes and productivity of the likes of Julian Champagnie, whose quick-trigger 3-point shooting has proven so vital for this iteration of the Spurs? Or Keldon Johnson, the reigning Sixth Man of the Year? Or Harrison Barnes, one of just two Spurs (along with Champagnie) knocking down at least 40% of his triples? Or second-year power forward Carter Bryant, whose ongoing development is a clear priority for San Antonio's future plans?

If Harris isn't able to hit the ground running — specifically by spacing the floor at a high level, as he did for Cade Cunningham in Detroit last season — it could throw some sand into the gears of a Spurs offense that has been humming despite not generating a ton from beyond the arc. San Antonio ranks just 26th in the league in the share of its shots that come from beyond the arc, and right around league-average in 3-point shooting accuracy.

That lagging 3-point attempt rate clearly hasn't hampered the offense's effectiveness thus far; some of it stems from the fact that the Spurs hammer the rim as frequently and effectively as nearly any team in the league. After finishing above league-average in 3-point attempt rate the last three seasons, though, you'd imagine Johnson would prefer to find ways to get a few more up — if for no other reason than to be prepared to have multiple styles to play when the postseason comes around and defensive game plans prioritize clogging the paint to take away Wembanyama's rolls to the rim and the three-headed guard monster's driving lanes to the basket.

If opposing defenses are able to congest the interior and force the Spurs to sing for their supper from outside, it'll bring to the forefront perhaps the most significant issue carrying over from last season: whether they have enough bankable 3-point shooting.

As it stands, the entire starting five — Wembanyama, Fox, Castle, Harper and Vassell — currently sits below 35% from deep for the season. Reigning Sixth Man of the Year Johnson is at 22.7%; erstwhile unicorn-turned-indoor cat Kornet hasn't attempted a long ball since April of 2025. The Spurs can make a lot of magic happen in tight confines, thanks to the size and brilliance of Wembanyama, and the speed, skill and force of their guards. If hardly anybody in the rotation can make a jumper when they need to, though, problems will arise.

Those issues — the bench minutes, the shooting, etc. — are not exactly surprises to the Spurs. They're well aware that they've got room to improve.

"If we felt like we're the best version of ourselves at this point in the season, we'll be in trouble," Keldon Johnson recently told reporters.

As excellent as their offense has been, the Spurs have actually underperformed their expected shot quality by the league's fifth-largest amount, according to Synergy Sports Technology's tracking — and all four teams above them in that ranking (Charlotte, Milwaukee, Utah, Chicago) have been terrible, without the talent to meaningfully bridge the gap between expectation and reality. That's certainly not the case in San Antonio.

If Wembanyama (35% from deep last season, 32% this season), Vassell (38% last season, 31% this season) and Johnson (36% last season, 23% this season) tick up toward their previous marks, and any of Fox, Harper or Castle nudge up toward league-average on their looks, this Spurs offense might have another level to reach. Honestly, it might even if only one of those guys keeps the arrow pointed north. You can probably guess which one.

"I can still do more," Wembanyama told reporters after his 52-point masterpiece against the Mavericks. "I mean, my shots weren't falling tonight and that forces me into a style of play that is exhausting. I can do it. I mean, the proof is here. I can do it, but I can be much better if my shots fall. I know it's just a matter of time."

If that happens — if the shots start to fall, the offense soars and the defense remains elite — then it might just be a matter of time before the Spurs are hoisting the Larry O'Brien Championship Trophy, too.

#2631. Fantasy Football Week 11 Panic Meter: Trey McBride's ceiling will be limited if Cardinals' offense continues to struggle

This week, I'm starting with the team that might surprise you because I've reached the point where there's nothing left to panic about.

New England totaled 151 net yards in a 35-10 loss to Detroit. Drake Maye exited on the opening drive, and Tommy DeVito completed 12 of 24 passes for 81 yards in relief. The passing game already offered little margin for error.

The bigger concern is Maye's ankle injury. Reports have raised the possibility that he could miss the remainder of the season, and Mike Vrabel doesn't expect him to be available immediately after the Week 11 bye. A season-ending absence isn't confirmed, but the fantasy playoff implications are serious.

That brings us to A.J. Brown. He's dealing with injuries of his own, and the temptation will be to put him right back into lineups whenever he's cleared. The numbers don't support it. Brown has 11 catches for 128 yards and no touchdowns in four games with Maye. DeVito doesn't improve that outlook.

Hunter Henry has a slightly different argument. Tight end has been a difficult position all season, and an inexperienced quarterback leaning on a veteran tight end makes sense in theory. But Henry's two catches against Detroit both came on the opening drive with Maye. He didn't record a reception from DeVito. He's a desperation option.

So, are Maye and Brown droppable in seasonal redraft leagues?

Maye is approaching that point if the injury timeline rules him out for the fantasy playoffs, particularly in leagues without an available IR spot. Brown is more dependent on league size and replacement options. In a standard 10- or 12-team league, moving on is reasonable if the waiver wire offers someone with a clearer path to usable production.

There's no obvious quarterback rescue coming for this passing game.

Panic Meter: NO PANIC. Expectations have already been reset. New England isn't an offense to chase for fantasy production until the situation changes.

Four targets for Chris Olave against Carolina. That's the number that stands out.

He finished with three catches for 30 yards, just one week after catching seven passes for 98 yards on 12 targets against Cleveland. The Cleveland game broke a streak of three straight outings under 60 yards.

Meanwhile, Jordyn Tyson caught 11 of 13 targets for 80 yards. The question is how Tyler Shough is distributing the ball, not whether Tyson has taken over.

Olave had reached double-digit targets in six of his first eight games. That volume helped offset the inconsistency of the Saints' passing attack and gave him a dependable path to fantasy points, even when the offense struggled. Fewer targets would widen his weekly range of outcomes.

One week doesn't establish a permanent shift, but Tyson's involvement is worth tracking. New Orleans doesn't consistently generate enough passing production to make an unexpected four-target afternoon easy to absorb.

Olave should remain in starting lineups. He still has the ability to produce strong fantasy weeks, and a single low-volume performance doesn't outweigh his season-long role.

Panic Meter: SOME PANIC. The concern isn't Olave's talent. It's whether the target advantage that has supported his production is becoming less reliable.

If you've watched the Rams' backfield recently, Blake Corum's explosiveness has been difficult to miss. Sean McVay has noticed too, praising Corum's twitch and explosiveness after his 100-yard performance against Arizona.

From Weeks 8 through 10, Corum rushed for 231 yards on 39 carries, averaging 5.9 yards per attempt. Kyren Williams totaled 124 yards on 43 carries, just 2.9 per attempt. Corum generated nearly twice the yardage on fewer opportunities.

Against Arizona, Corum finished with 100 yards and a touchdown on 17 carries. Williams managed 23 rushing yards on 12 attempts. The Rams won comfortably, but the backs had very different afternoons.

Williams still matters to this offense. His work in pass protection and the passing game gives him a role that doesn't disappear because Corum has been more efficient on the ground. The question is how much of the rushing workload he can retain while Corum keeps producing.

There's no confirmed depth-chart change, but the old workload assumptions deserve another look. Corum has given the coaching staff a reason to keep him involved.

The Week 11 bye gives Los Angeles time to evaluate its rotation. Watch the touch distribution coming out of it rather than assuming the old split automatically returns.

Panic Meter: SOME PANIC+. Williams is still a viable fantasy starter, but his weekly ceiling is getting harder to project with Corum earning more work.

Detroit scored 35 points against New England, and Sam LaPorta caught one pass for 16 yards.

That sums up the problem. The Lions' offense can function at a high level without LaPorta making much of an impact in the box score.

Over his last four games, LaPorta has nine receptions for 99 yards and no touchdowns on 16 targets. The opportunities haven't been there. Jahmyr Gibbs and Amon-Ra St. Brown remain central to the offense, and Detroit has enough ways to score without featuring its tight end.

For fantasy managers, that leaves LaPorta heavily dependent on touchdowns. It's a difficult way to operate at an already volatile position, especially when he hasn't found the end zone in four straight games.

There's reason for patience. Detroit routinely creates scoring opportunities, so a usage increase could turn into a productive week quickly. The problem is identifying when that usage is actually coming.

LaPorta shouldn't be viewed as an unquestioned starter based only on the quality of his offense. Matchups and available alternatives matter more now than they did earlier in the season.

Panic Meter: SOME PANIC. Detroit's scoring potential keeps the upside alive, but it hasn't protected LaPorta's weekly floor.

Trey McBride caught every pass thrown his way Sunday. There were only five.

He finished with five receptions for 37 yards against the Rams, but Arizona's overall performance tells the bigger story. The Cardinals ran 34 offensive plays, earned six first downs and failed on all six third-down attempts.

Carson Beck threw for 108 yards with two interceptions in his first NFL start. Arizona scored six points and has managed just nine over its last two games. That's not enough sustained offense to support reliable fantasy production, regardless of how good McBride is at earning targets.

When drives end after a few snaps, even a strong target share means limited opportunities. McBride didn't lose his role. Arizona simply couldn't keep its offense on the field.

Total Panic would be premature. Beck drew a difficult Rams matchup in his debut, and one start isn't enough to determine what the passing game will look like over the final stretch. Kansas City is next, so the evaluation won't get easier, but the rookie deserves another opportunity before his impact on McBride is treated as settled.

The comparison with LaPorta is useful. Detroit can score without feeding LaPorta. Arizona needs McBride involved, but its offense hasn't been able to sustain drives. Same position, very different paths to disappointing fantasy results.

McBride should remain in starting lineups. Very few tight ends combine his talent with his share of their team's passing opportunities. The production may be inconsistent until Arizona improves, but benching him would create a different kind of risk.

Panic Meter: SOME PANIC. Give Beck another start. If Arizona continues to struggle to move the chains, McBride's ceiling will be limited by the offense around him.

#2630. Former Bucs second-round pick delivers two-sack performance

Former Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive lineman Logan Hall is putting together a productive stretch with the Houston Texans. Hall recorded two sacks in Sunday's 27-24 loss to the Cleveland Browns, bringing his season total to four. NFL reporter Greg Auman highlighted the performance, which gave Hall three sacks over his last two games.

Hall finished with two solo tackles against Cleveland, both coming on sacks of quarterback Deshaun Watson. The plays resulted in a combined loss of 21 yards, including an 11-yard sack that pushed Cleveland backward. It was Hall's second career game with multiple sacks and his first since joining Houston.

Through nine appearances with the Texans, Hall has recorded 14 combined tackles, including eight solo tackles and six assists, along with four sacks. He has not started a game this season, but his sack production has already surpassed his final year in Tampa Bay.

The Buccaneers selected Hall with the 33rd overall pick in the second round of the 2022 NFL Draft. He spent four seasons with Tampa Bay, totaling 10 sacks across 66 games. His most productive season as a pass rusher came in 2024, when he recorded a career-high 5.5 sacks. That production dropped to 1.5 sacks in 2025, despite Hall starting 16 of 17 games and recording a career-high 39 tackles.

Hall joined Houston during the 2026 offseason and has recorded three of his four sacks in the last two games, including one against the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 9. His four sacks in nine appearances are already 2.5 more than he managed across 17 games with Tampa Bay last season.

Hall started 16 games for Tampa Bay last season and finished with 1.5 sacks. He hasn't started a game for Houston this year but already has four sacks in nine appearances. That puts him just 1.5 sacks away from matching his career high of 5.5, which he set with the Buccaneers in 2024.

This article originally appeared on Bucs Wire: Former Bucs second-round pick delivers two-sack performance

#2628. Eagles News: The MVP of Philadelphia’s season thus far

Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

You know you're not in a good place when the punter is the MVP. Do you agree with this pick of Braden Mann? Or would you go with another player? From an entertainment standpoint, Howie Roseman has a case as the MVP since the Cam Jurgens and Jordan Davis are two of the more exciting moments of the season. Or you could go with Jalen Hurts since he was a big reason the team won the only two games they did and have looked very lost without him.

Let's get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

NFL Power Rankings: Stacking all 32 teams for Week 11, plus non-QB MVPs – ESPN

28) Philadelphia Eagles (2-7). Non-QB MVP at midseason: P Braden Mann. Mann has been called on more than any other punter, which is what happens when your offense leads the league in three-and-outs by a healthy margin. But he has been nails for the most part. Mann has an NFL-best 22 punts inside the 20-yard line and only two touchbacks. His 86-yard boot in Week 9 against the Giants was the second-longest punt since 2000. And no, it is not a good sign when your punter is your first-half MVP.

As for the team that Eagles fans should prefer to win the division, assuming it's not going to be Philly? I previously felt like the Giants were the answer to this question because I can see them beating their chests about barely winning a bad division and overestimating how close they are to being serious contenders. But I actually think Washington might be the preferable choice. Maybe the Commanders keep Dan Quinn and put too much stock into coming back to win the NFC East, only to then struggle again in 2027. What do you think?

NFC East Mixtape VOL. 207: Is Washington a real threat to win this? – NFC East Mixtape

Week 11 odds: Steelers open as favorites vs. Eagles – Behind The Steel Curtain

The Steelers have not won in Philadelphia since October 24, 1965. Their last victory came before the Super Bowl era, the Penguins were founded, the Pirates won their last two World Series titles, and NFL and AFL merged. Pittsburgh needs a win to keep pace with the Bengals and hold off the Cleveland Browns, who are making a charge in the AFC Wild Card race. The Steelers look to prevent a snowball effect after a crushing Cincinnati loss that could be the turning point of the 2026 season.

Eagles 'soft tank' roadmap for the remainder of the 2026 season – PhillyVoice

5) Get a head start on a plan for the 2027 coaching staff. Jeffrey Lurie and Howie Roseman are going to have to decide which coaches are out after this season, and which coaches they would like to retain. Of course, the biggest decision will be whether or not to move on from head coach Nick Sirianni. A few weeks ago, we laid out the argument for both sides, and in my opinion, there's a stronger case for moving on. The last time the Eagles fired a head coach was after the 2020 season, when Doug Pederson was unable to survive a 4-11-1 record. That situation was a little different in that the Eagles didn't decide to fire Pederson until after the season had ended, when Pederson wasn't amenable to other changes within his coaching staff. If the Eagles are going to move on from Sirianni, they should probably already know by now. And if that is the intent, they'll be in a unique position — relative to past firings, anyway — where they can formulate a head coaching search plan well in advance of the actual firing of the current head coach. I have no inside information here, but I would be stunned if early conversations on potential replacements aren't already underway.

QB Drew Mestemaker – Oklahoma State – The Eagles have a big decision to make about Jalen Hurts future. Is he the QB for 2027? Do they sign him to an extension? We'll see how that plays out. They could decide to go for a QB at 5 because you don't often get a shot to draft that high. The QB could sit for a few years if needed. Mestemaker leads an explosive offense at OSU and he's had a terrific season. He is a good athlete who can make some really impressive throws.

Questions by position as Eagles return from 2026 bye week – NBCSP

Coaching: Will Nick Sirianni survive this season? This season has been ugly. The Eagles won their first two games and have now lost seven straight. Sure, they lost Jalen Hurts for the season and have dealt with countless other injuries, so it has been a weird year. Maybe Jeffrey Lurie looks at the situation and gives Sirianni a mulligan. After all, Sirianni has been to the playoffs five times, to the Super Bowl twice and won it all to cap the 2024 season. That wasn't that long ago. But we have also seen Lurie fire a Super Bowl-winning head coach and explain that it wasn't because Doug Pederson deserved to get fired; he moved on in 2021 because he thought it was in the best interest of the franchise. So Lurie has to look at this situation and determine if the best thing for the franchise is to run it back with Sirianni in 2027. And if he does that, who are his coordinators? It's hard to imagine Sirianni getting fired before the end of the season, so those are all fair questions for January. In the interim, let's just see if the players continue to fight for Sirianni and his future.

Are the Eagles, Howie Roseman entering the quarterback wilderness without Jalen Hurts? – PHLY Eagles

Let's assume the answer to both of those questions is yes. Wouldn't another year spent trying to maximize Hurts with a rebuilt offensive line and quite possibly a different coaching staff give you about as much of a chance to find a "franchise quarterback" in Hurts as drafting the second or third quarterback prospect available this year? The Eagles also have plenty of draft capital in 2028 and 2029 with a real chance that the likes of Mestemaker, Manning, Mensah, and Co. will actually feature in a draft class, although it's no given that draft capital will actually allow them to get in position for a highly touted prospect. All of this to say, the Eagles may be entering the quarterback wilderness whether they like it or not. But the notion that they should do so willingly or with enthusiasm loses sight of how difficult it may be to actually replace the most accomplished quarterback in franchise history.

Colts sign CB Johnathan Edwards to active roster from practice squad; sign WR Samori Toure to practice squad – Colts

Toure, 6-1, 196 pounds, has played in 23 career games (two starts) in his time with the Philadelphia Eagles (2026), New Orleans Saints (2025), Denver Broncos (2025), Chicago Bears (2024-25) and Green Bay Packers (2022-24). He has compiled 14 receptions for 163 yards (11.6 avg.) and one touchdown. Toure was originally selected by the Packers in the seventh round (258th overall) of the 2022 NFL Draft out of Nebraska. His name is pronounced suh-MORE-ee TOO-ray.

Rams' injuries provide silver lining of depth chart changes – Turf Show Times

Poor [former Eagles center] Dylan McMahon, he gets a shot at his first extended action since Week 18 of the 2024 season and gets hurt.

Packers WR clears waivers, set up for practice squad return – Acme Packing Company

Notably, the Packers have an open spot on their practice squad, as the team just released [former Eagles] defensive lineman David Blay Jr. from the 17-man unit.

NY Giants cut struggling kick returner, sign another shaky one – Big Blue View

Xavier Gipson is being signed off the Philadelphia Eagles' practice squad. This will actually be Gipson's third time as a Giant. He was claimed off waivers from the New York Jets in 2025, then lost to the Eagles. He was re-signed to the practice squad late last season, and was with the team throughout training camp before being released in final roster cuts. Gipson, 25, has extensive experience as a returner. He has averaged 9.1 yards on 74 punt returns and 25.9 yards on 51 kickoff returns. Gipson's issue has always been ball security. He has 12 fumbles in 163 career touches, one every 13.6 touches, and has lost jobs with the Jets and Eagles largely because of those issues. If the Giants are looking for added ball security, turning to Gipson is risky.

AT&T Stadium has become a house of horrors for Cowboys – Blogging The Boys

AT&T Stadium has become a house of horrors. This was true before a snap had been taken. Well before kickoff it was obvious that the Cowboys had absolutely no home field advantage to speak of on Sunday as 49ers fans had full well taken over AT&T Stadium.

Washington's offensive identity is beginning to take shape | Commanders Film Session – Hogs Haven

The Washington Commanders handled the New York Giants' pressure packages significantly better than they did in their first matchup in Week 5, and the improvement stemmed from several areas. Offensive coordinator David Blough was more willing to move the pocket, particularly in down-and-distance situations where Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson typically dialed up pressure. Jayden Daniels and Nick Allegretti did an excellent job setting protections, but perhaps most importantly, Daniels consistently identified answers pre-snap and delivered the football within the timing of the offense. According to SumerSports, Washington's pressure rate dropped from 46 percent (seventh-worst in the NFL) in its Week 5 matchup against New York to 23 percent in Week 10, the third-best mark in the NFL that week. However, Washington's offensive performance against the Giants was about more than its ability to handle pressure. For an offense that has struggled with consistency throughout the season, Thursday night offered some indication that Washington may finally be developing an identity through the strengths of its personnel.

Updated NFL Draft order after Chargers get first win vs. Ravens – SB Nation

The Los Angeles Chargers have their first win of the season, moving to 1-8 after a 23-20 victory over the Baltimore Ravens on Monday Night Football. As a result, the Tennessee Titans now have the first pick in the 2027 NFL Draft.

Philadelphia announced as host of 4 additional Army-Navy games through 2034 – CBS News

Philadelphia is hosting four more Army-Navy games into 2034, officials announced Tuesday. The games will take place at Lincoln Financial Field in 2028, 2030, 2032 and 2034, the directors of athletics at the U.S. Naval Academy and U.S. Military Academy said.

Ward has also done this without his top receiver Carnell Tate, who's missed the last two outings but is expected to return for their Week 11 matchup with the Cowboys. It's the right time to get back since Tennessee is third in neutral pace of play and Dallas leads the league in that category — setting up a massive opportunity for fantasy scoring.

It's also worth noting that Ward has one of the five easiest fantasy schedules for QBs the rest of the way, including matchups with the Commanders (Week 13), Lions (Week 14), Colts (Week 15) and Raiders (Week 16). Though I'm still only valuing Ward as a fantasy QB2 streamer, don't be surprised if we see the former first-round pick finish hot down the stretch.

Desperation streaming options (if starter is out)

Black has been one of the stars of this column all season long and the fact that he's still available in over 60% of fantasy leagues is a massive mistake by managers.

Just look at what happened with Emmett Johnson last week, when Kenneth Walker III got hurt in practice. The Chiefs' rookie stepped into the starting role and delivered 171 scrimmage yards and two touchdowns. That's the kind of upside Black offers if Christian McCaffrey were ever to miss time.

Even with CMC active, Black's role has grown in recent weeks resulting in 59 yards and TD in Week 7, a bye in Week 8, 70 yards in Week 9 and 68 yards and a TD last week. Most importantly, he's been given at least 11 touches in each of those games. When you're playing in one of the best offenses in the NFL, that kind of volume makes you a strong RB3/flex option with weekly RB2 upside when you find the end zone.

Don't let Black remain on the waiver wire any longer, he should be rostered in 100% of leagues.

Baker Mayfield is banged up and might sit out this week, which would put Jalon Daniels back under center. The rookie performed well in his three starts earlier in the season, but be prepared for the Bucs offense to lean even heavier on the run.

Gainwell has displayed weekly RB3/flex value over the last three games with 88 yards in Week 7, 140 yards in Week 8 and 76 yards in Week 9 before the team went on bye.

Bucky Irving is the unquestioned starter in Tampa Bay's backfield, but Gainwell needs to be rostered everywhere as a flex option with RB1 upside if injuries strike.

Even after a potential Jonathan Taylor trade failed to materialize, the Colts continued to split RB volume with the veteran turning his 18 touches into 103 scrimmage yards and McGowan chipping in with 77 yards and a TD on 12 opportunities.

It's the second consecutive game where the rookie reached the end zone, making him a legitimate RB3/flex option in fantasy, even as Taylor's running mate.

We could also see the team shut Taylor down at some point in the final two months, if he gets even the slightest injury. There's no reason to risk your star on a team that's going nowhere. If that occurs, McGowan would be a fantasy RB2 in whatever games he starts.

Woody Marks suffered a concussion and is unlikely to be cleared before Thursday's game against the Colts. David Montgomery, who hasn't suited up since Week 5 due to a groin injury, returned to practice last week and put in a full session on Friday, but was ultimately ruled out for the game. That puts Montgomery on track to potentially play against the Colts, unless he suffered a setback.

If Montgomery can't go, then Demercado would be the next man up. He's earned 15 touches while playing behind Marks the last two games, only managing 39 scoreless scrimmage yards. In that scenario, Demercado would be a volume-based fantasy RB3.

Jacory Croskey-Merritt is 52% rostered but would be the No. 3 RB add, if available.

Chris Rodriguez Jr. at NYG (37% rostered)

It's easy to forget, but Bryant had a growing role in the Broncos' passing attack during the opening month before being placed on injured reserve with an ankle injury. In those first four games, Bryant topped 40 yards three times.

So, it was great to see him post a season-high 56 yards and a touchdown on four catches in his first game back since the injury. Jaylen Waddle also suffered a concussion, but he should be cleared coming off Denver's Week 10 bye.

Regardless, Bryant was a borderline flex option early in the season and has returned with an even better performance. Given Waddle's struggles and Courtland Sutton's age, there's a non-zero chance Bryant becomes the most valuable fantasy receiver in Denver for the rest of the season.

While CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens get all the headlines, Flournoy has become a very consistent contributor in the Cowboys' passing attack.

The 27-year-old has at least 50 yards and/or a touchdown in six straight games, finishing as a top-24 fantasy WR in five of those outings.

Even as the third pass-catcher in Dallas, Flournoy can be started in fantasy as a WR3/flex option, especially in an uptempo contest against a Titans defense allowing the most points to wideouts.

Despite not earning the kind of volume we'd like to see from a full-time receiver, Williams has been productive most weeks. The rookie has at least 50 yards or a touchdown in three of his last four games since Terry McLaurin was lost for the season.

Until he sees more consistent targets, it's hard to trust Williams as anything more than a flex option. With Stefon Diggs drawing the attention of top corners, Williams could earn more volume during that span.

Mitchell's outlook is complicated. Omar Cooper Jr. is dealing with an ankle injury that could sideline him for a few games. That would condense the crowded receiver room down to Mitchell and Garrett Wilson, making Mitchell a possible WR3/flex option in fantasy.

Unfortunately, Geno Smith also suffered an ankle injury that might sideline him. Rookie backup Cade Klubnik represents a significant downgrade that would lower the ceiling of all the skill positions players in New York's offense.

So, Mitchell is a tentative add who could be started if Cooper misses time and if Smith doesn't. The fact that I'm writing about him in the waiver wire column is a clear sign we've reached Week 11 and the pickups are getting thin.

#2626. Kings are 1-12 and coaching rumors have begun. Two familiar names are surfacing.

The Sacramento Kings are off to a 1-12 start that has started heating up the coach's rumor mill.

The Kings are led by second-year head coach Doug Christie, who took over the position in December 2024 after Sacramento fired Mike Brown. After Christie lead Sacramento to a 27-24 record, the Kings removed the interim tag in April 2025.

Since then, Christie has a 23-72 record, leading to speculation of an eventual coaching change.

According to NBA insider Marc Stein, there are already rumbles in league coaching circles that have named both Tom Thibodeau and Mark Jackson as "potential down-the-road" head coaching candidates for the Kings, if Sacramento eventually makes a coaching change.

More: Kings head coach Doug Christie gets brutally honest about job security

Both candidates would be intriguing, however, the Kings have indicated they have no plans to move on, as they are hesitant to fire Christie, according to The Athletic's Sam Amick.

Thibodeau is a two-time NBA Coach of the Year in 2011 and 2021 and is known for coaching defensive-focused teams that had perennial regular-season success and playoff appearances with the Chicago Bulls, Minnesota Timberwolves and New York Knicks. The Kings have a dynamic point guard in Darius Acuff Jr. and Thibodeau is no stranger to talented point guards having coached Derrick Rose and Jalen Brunson.

Jackson coached the Golden State Warriors for three seasons from 2011 to 2014. He hasn't coached since but has often been credited with helping build the foundation of the future Warriors dynasty led by Stephen Curry, Klay Thompson and Draymond Green. When the Warriors were an afterthought in the league, Jackson's coaching, eye for talent and how to maximize it helped the Warriors become a playoff team before they ascended into a championship team under Steve Kerr.

Christie addressed hot seat rumors after the Kings' Nov. 13 loss to the Portland Trail Blazers.

"I think this seat is hot always, so it doesn't really matter," Christie told USA TODAY. "Obviously, we want to win games. Nobody wants to win more than me, from the standpoint that the record doesn't go on the player's numbers. The record goes on coach's number."

Christie is in the final year of a guaranteed contract. He signed a three-year deal for approximately $2 million a year with the final year (2027-28) a team option.

Sacramento is Christie's first position as a head coach in the NBA. He was the Kings' assistant coach from 2021 to 2024, including the original "Beam Team" that ended a 16-year playoff drought in 2023.

Christie played for seven teams in a 15-season NBA career, including as a starter and defensive enforcer with the Kings during their best era in the early 2000s. Christie made the NBA All-Defensive First Team once and the NBA All-Defensive Second Team three times during his Kings tenure between 2000 and 2005.

#2625. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B
